lessons.title: Indian Equities: Long-Run Nifty Returns, Drawdowns and Recovery Times

children.text: Every alternative asset you will meet in this course gets sold against one benchmark: "better than the stock market." So before you judge any of them, you need an honest picture of what Indian equities have actually delivered. Not the brochure version ("the Nifty has compounded at double digits"), and not the panic version ("the market can wipe you out"). The real version: the returns, the worst falls, and how long it took to get your money back. This lesson builds that benchmark using the Nifty 50.

body.text: Indian equities have rewarded patient investors with strong long-run returns, but they charge for it in full view: falls of 40 to 60% that can take years to recover. Every alternative should be judged against both halves of that deal.

markDefs.definition: A version of an index that assumes all dividends paid by its companies are reinvested. It shows the full return an investor would have earned, not just the price change.

children.text: The Nifty 50 closed 1999 at about 1,480 and closed 2024 at about 23,645. That is a price return of roughly 11.7% a year over 25 years. The index level ignores dividends, which have historically added around 1 to 1.5 percentage points a year. The
includes them, and it is the fairer figure to compare with any alternative that pays you income.
That 11.7% hides a very uneven ride. Here is what the Nifty 50 did, year by year, from the 2008 crash onwards.

body.title: Nifty 50 calendar-year price returns, 2008 to 2024 (%, approximate)

children.text: In those 17 years, the Nifty lost money in three calendar years, and only once did it deliver a return close to its long-run average. "12% a year" is what equity compounds to over time, not what it pays you each year.

body.text: Your starting point changes everything. Someone who bought at the end of 2007, near the peak, earned a price CAGR of only about 8.3% to the end of 2024. Someone who bought one year later, at the end of 2008, earned about 13.9%. Same index, same end date, very different outcomes.

markDefs.definition: The percentage fall from a previous peak to the lowest point before a new peak is reached. The largest such fall over a period is the maximum drawdown.

children.text: Volatility tells you how bumpy the ride is. A
tells you how much of your money disappeared from the top before things turned. For most investors, drawdowns are what risk actually feels like.

body.caption: Major Nifty 50 drawdowns and recovery times (closing prices, before dividends, approximate)

children.text: Remember this is the Nifty 50, India's 50 largest companies. Mid-cap and small-cap indices have historically fallen much further in the same episodes, with small caps losing well over 60% in 2008. Recovery times would also be longer after inflation, since getting back to the old index level is not the same as getting back your purchasing power.

body.caption: Loss expressed as a decimal, e.g. 0.50 for a 50% fall

children.text: A 50% fall needs a 100% gain just to break even. The 2020 fall of about 38.4% needed a gain of about 62%. That is why deep drawdowns take so long to recover from, and why an asset whose losses you cannot see is not necessarily an asset that has none.

body.title: Climbing back from 2008
body.prompt: The Nifty 50 fell about 60% from its January 2008 peak to its October 2008 bottom. What percentage gain was needed from the bottom just to get back to the peak?
body.explanation: 1 ÷ (1 − 0.60) − 1 = 1 ÷ 0.40 − 1 = 1.5, or 150%. The index had to more than double and then go halfway again, which is why full recovery took until late 2010.

children.text: Time in the Market: Why Holding Period Matters

Historically, the longer you held the Nifty 50, the smaller your chance of a loss and the narrower the range of outcomes. The ranges below are broad and approximate, but the pattern has held across Indian market history since the late 1990s.

body.caption: How holding period has changed the Nifty 50 experience (approximate historical pattern)
headers: What the range of outcomes looked like

cells: From a loss of about half to a gain of over 75%
From modest annual losses to very strong gains
Rare, mostly for buyers near the 2008 peak
From roughly flat to high teens a year
No losing 10-year periods on price since the late 1990s
From around 5% a year to well above 15% a year

children.text: This matters when you compare with alternatives. A PE fund or a flat is usually held for 7 to 10 years. The fair comparison is not the Nifty's scary one-year range, but its 7 to 10-year range, where the chance of loss has historically been small. Alternatives often win the argument by comparing their long-horizon returns with the market's short-horizon risk.

Try the calculator: a ₹20,000 monthly SIP for 15 years at 12% a year, then again at 8%. The gap shows how much the long-run return assumption matters, and why an alternative promising a few extra points deserves serious scrutiny rather than instant belief.

body.title: The Nifty 50 index fund as a benchmark for alternatives

columns.label: What it offers
points: Long-run price returns of about 11.7% a year since 1999, plus dividends
A live price and exit on any trading day
Costs that can be well under 0.2% a year for direct index funds and ETFs
No manager selection risk and full daily transparency
LTCG taxed at 12.5% above ₹1.25 lakh a year after one year

columns.label: What it demands
points: Stomaching visible falls of 40 to 60% in severe bear markets
Waiting up to about four years for prices to recover
Holding through years with flat or negative returns
Not selling in a panic, which is harder than it sounds
Accepting that starting valuations shape your return

body.text: Equity's biggest risk is usually the investor, not the index. The drawdowns above only become permanent losses when people sell near the bottom. An alternative that stops you from panic-selling can look better partly because it removes the option to make that mistake.

body.title: A fair comparison
body.question: A real estate AIF with a 7-year life says: "The Nifty lost 38% in 2020. Our fund never had a negative year." What is the fairest way to compare the two?
options: Compare the fund's best year with the Nifty's worst year
Compare the fund's net return over 7 years with the Nifty 50 TRI over the same 7 years, allowing for smoothing and liquidity
Compare only annual volatility, since that measures risk
Accept the claim, because never having a negative year proves lower risk
body.explanation: The fund is a 7-year commitment, so the fair benchmark is the Nifty's return over the same 7 years, including dividends. Then adjust for the facts that the fund's values are appraised and that you could not have exited it, while the index fund could be sold any day.

body.title: Name the measure
body.textWithBlank: The largest percentage fall from a peak to a trough over a given period is called the maximum ___.
body.explanation: Maximum drawdown captures the worst loss an investor who bought at the top would have sat through. For the Nifty 50 since 2000, that was about 60% in 2008.

body.title: Suresh sells in March 2020
body.scenario: Suresh, a 50-year-old bank manager in Nagpur, invested ₹10 lakh in a Nifty 50 index fund on 14 January 2020, when the index closed at about 12,362. On 23 March 2020 it closed at about 7,610, and he sold everything and moved the money to a savings account. The index ended 2020 at about 13,982. Ignore dividends, costs and tax.
body.prompt: What was Suresh's investment worth when he sold, and what would it have been worth at the end of 2020 if he had held on? What does this tell you about how to compare equities with alternatives?
body.modelAnswer:
When he sold: ₹10 lakh × 7,610 ÷ 12,362 ≈ ₹6.16 lakh, a loss of about 38%.

If he had held to the end of 2020: ₹10 lakh × 13,982 ÷ 12,362 ≈ ₹11.31 lakh, a gain of about 13% in under a year.

The difference, about ₹5.15 lakh, came entirely from his decision, not from the market.

What it tells you:
1. Equity drawdowns are visible and frightening, and they tempt people into locking in losses.
2. The same crash, measured by an appraised alternative, might have shown a small dip and no sale. That can lead to better investor behaviour, but it does not mean the underlying asset was safer.
3. When comparing, ask two separate questions: which asset has the better risk and return, and which one will I actually hold through a crisis?

body.label: Nifty Indices: Historical Data
body.description: Download official historical price and Total Return Index data for the Nifty 50 and other NSE indices to check any return claim yourself.

points: The Nifty 50's price return was about 11.7% a year from 1999 to 2024, with dividends adding roughly 1 to 1.5 points more.
Annual returns swung from −51.8% in 2008 to +75.8% in 2009. The long-run average is what equity compounds to, not what it pays each year.
Major drawdowns have ranged from about 16% to 60%, taking from about ten months to nearly four years to recover on price.
A loss of 60% needs a gain of 150% to break even, which is why deep falls take so long to repair.
Over 10-year holding periods, the Nifty has historically not lost money on price since the late 1990s, so compare long-lock-in alternatives with long-horizon equity returns.
Equity is the benchmark because its risk is fully visible, and alternatives should be judged against both its return and its liquidity.
